fields.questionText:
A school organised a lottery for its 100 students. A box contains 100 tickets, one for each student, of which 25 are winning tickets. Each student draws one ticket at random, and a drawn ticket is not put back. Answer the following:
(i) What is the probability that the first student draws a winning ticket?
(ii) What is the probability that the first student draws a losing ticket?
(iii) After 10 winning and 15 losing tickets have been drawn, what is the probability that the next student draws a winning ticket? Also find the probability that this student draws a losing ticket.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Total tickets = 100, winning = 25, so P(winning) = 25/100 = 1/4
[1 mark] (iii) Tickets left = 100 − 25 = 75; winning left = 25 − 10 = 15; losing left = 75 − 15 = 60

rationale: Stem now states 100 tickets (25 winning), draws without return, and (iii) asks for a specific event. Restructured to (i)(ii)(iii) 1+1+2. Dropped (iv) (trivial check).

fields.questionText:
In a survey on holidays, 120 people were asked to state which type of transport they used on their last holiday. The results are shown in a pie chart with these sector angles: Bus 36°, Ship 33°, Car 177°. The remaining 114° of the chart is made up of the Train and Aeroplane sectors. Answer the following questions:
(i) If one person is selected at random, find the probability that he/she travelled by bus or ship.
(ii) Which is the most favourite mode of transport and how many people used it?
(iii) (a) A person is selected at random. If the probability that he did not use train is 4/5, find the number of people who used train.
OR
(iii) (b) The probability that a randomly selected person used aeroplane is 7/60. Find the revenue collected by the air company at the rate of ₹5,000 per person.
fields.answer: (i) 23/120 (ii) Car, 59 people (iii)(a) 24 people OR (iii)(b) 14 people used aeroplane; revenue = 14 × 5000 = ₹70,000

rationale: Stem de-spaced, mark numbers and footer removed. The pie is described only by the angles in the row's own steps (36°, 33°, 177°) and its answers (train + aeroplane = 24 + 14 people = 114°). The answer field now holds all the parts.

At an elementary school level, computer applications can be used to display multimedia lesson plans. A survey was done on 1000 elementary and secondary schools of Assam and they were classified by the number of computers they had:
Number of computers: 1–10 | 11–20 | 21–50 | 51–100 | 101 and more
Number of schools: 250 | 200 | 290 | 180 | 80
One school is chosen at random. Then:
(i) Find the probability that the school chosen at random has more than 100 computers.
(ii) (a) Find the probability that the school chosen at random has 50 or fewer computers.

(iii) Find the probability that the school chosen at random has 10 or fewer computers.

fields.questionText:
A school is organising a raffle draw in which 100 tickets are sold, numbered 1 to 100. Ramesh buys 2 of these tickets. One ticket is drawn at random for the first prize.
(i) What is the probability that the drawn ticket is one of Ramesh's tickets?
(ii) What is the probability that the drawn ticket is not one of Ramesh's tickets?
(iii) The school decides that the 5 tickets numbered 96 to 100 are reserved for teachers and removes them before the draw. Ramesh's tickets are not among them. Find the new probability that Ramesh wins the first prize, and the probability that he does not.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] (i) Total outcomes = 100, favourable = 2, so P = 2/100 = 1/50
[1 mark] (iii) Tickets left in the draw = 100 − 5 = 95, of which Ramesh holds 2
[1 mark] (iii) P(Ramesh wins) = 2/95, so P(does not win) = 1 − 2/95 = 93/95

rationale: Authored row. The two-ticket without-replacement compound probability is beyond 'simple problems'. Rewritten as single-draw events, 1+1+2, with the complement kept.
